from pathlib import Path

    texts.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n{t}')

strengths: MaskSub offers a simple, technically coherent way to combine supervised learning with strong masking: a shared-weight masked branch learns from detached predictions of the unmasked branch. It adds no inference overhead and integrates with established training recipes.

The main accuracy improvements are well supported across architectures and training settings. Table 1 reports gains of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across ViT sizes and training lengths; Tables 3 and 5 extend the evidence to pretrained models, ResNets, and Swin Transformers.

The computational comparisons support practical usefulness. In Table 7, ViT-B with MaskSub achieves 84.1% using 25 GPU-days, versus 83.7% for longer baseline training using 26 GPU-days. Table 8 also demonstrates a favorable accuracy–cost tradeoff against CoSub.

The contribution extends beyond ImageNet classification. The appendix reports improvements on ADE20K segmentation, COCO detection and instance segmentation, and multiple distribution-shift benchmarks. For example, ViT-B ImageNet-A accuracy increases from 36.8% to 41.9%.

Mask-ratio and loss-weight ablations, three-run statistics for several central experiments, concise pseudocode, detailed training configurations, and a code link support reproducibility. This empirical breadth provides the main basis for weak acceptance.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the method combines established masking and asymmetric self-distillation ideas, with close connections to CoSub and GradAug. Although Tables 8–9 provide useful comparisons, Table 6 compares different training recipes and cannot establish the claimed incompatibility of earlier self-distillation methods with strong recipes.

The automatic difficulty-control explanation exceeds the evidence. Equation (3) applies distillation to every example and does not check whether the teacher is correct; confidently incorrect predictions can still provide strong targets. Figure 3 supports a changing aggregate gradient contribution, but does not establish the claimed exclusive application to successfully learned examples.

The benefits are conditional. Table 10 shows ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy falling from 91.7% to 89.6% when MaskSub is used in both pretraining and fine-tuning. Section 4.2 also states that CLIP's best-checkpoint accuracy is unchanged, so its reported improvement concerns the final checkpoint. These results qualify the broad claims of consistent gains.

Statistical support is uneven. The repeated-run results substantiate important DeiT experiments, but the 0.1-point BEiTv2 improvements and small dense-prediction gains lack corresponding uncertainty estimates. Additionally, Table A.6 does not clearly specify whether 'without KD loss' replaces the masked branch's target with ground truth or removes its loss, limiting interpretation of that ablation.

There are correctable reporting issues. Table 9 gives 8.6 versus 23.4 GPU-days, approximately 37% of total training cost, whereas the text claims one sixth without distinguishing incremental from total cost. Table 10 labels the ViT-S Cars increase from 80.9% to 92.2% as +1.3 instead of +11.3 points. These errors warrant correction but do not overturn the main empirical contribution.
